chief_complaint: headaches, transient vision loss, and bilateral papilledema
hpi_details: A 34-year-old female presents to the clinic with headaches, transient visual obscurations, and bilateral papilledema that have gradually worsened.
ideas: She thinks she might have a brain tumor or a dangerous eye disease that is putting pressure on her optic nerves.
concerns: She is worried that these momentary blackouts will turn into permanent blindness and leave her unable to drive or care for her family.
expectations: She hopes to get an immediate head scan and a direct referral to an eye specialist today.

investigation_events.title: Urgent MRI/MRV and opening-pressure assessment
investigation_events.availability_message: Urgent MRI/MRV and lumbar puncture results are now available. Lumbar puncture was performed only after imaging excluded a mass lesion and venous sinus thrombosis.

results.value: No intracranial mass, hydrocephalus, or venous sinus thrombosis; partially empty sella and bilateral transverse sinus narrowing

results.note: Measured in the lateral decubitus position; CSF constituents are normal.

clinical_knowledge.topic: Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension (Pseudotumor Cerebri) evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension (Pseudotumor Cerebri) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes Plan for Pseudotumor Cerebri: Brain MRI/MRV, lumbar puncture, Acetazolamide, weight loss, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: headaches, transient vision loss, and bilateral papilledema
Key HPI features: A 34-year-old female presents to the clinic with headaches, transient visual obscurations, and bilateral papilledema that have gradually worsened.
Objective/Exam findings: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Pseudotumor Cerebri.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension (Pseudotumor Cerebri).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Progressive vision loss.
management_principles: Plan for Pseudotumor Cerebri: Brain MRI/MRV, lumbar puncture, Acetazolamide, weight loss
Arrange urgent ophthalmology and neurology assessment to protect vision
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

teaching.one_liner: Elevated brain pressure without a mass, causing headaches, transient vision loss, and bilateral papilledema.

must_ask.say: Is the headache worse in the morning or with straining?
Do you have brief episodes of vision going dark?
Any whooshing sound in your ears?
Any new medications, like acne treatments or birth control?

history.answer: I have been having persistent headaches for the past month, and recently my vision keeps completely blacking out for a couple of seconds whenever I bend over or stand up.
The headaches started gradually about a month ago and have slowly but steadily become more severe and constant over the last two weeks.
Right now the headache occurs every day, lasting for most of the day rather than coming in short attacks.
It feels diffuse all over my head, but the dull aching pressure is most intense behind my eyes and across my forehead on both sides.
It feels like a heavy, throbbing pressure building inside my head. On a ten-point scale, it is usually around a six or seven.
It is definitely worst in the early morning when I first wake up, and sometimes the throbbing pain even wakes me up early.
The head pressure gets noticeably worse whenever I cough, sneeze, strain, or bend over to tie my shoes. Resting with my head elevated eases it slightly, but lying flat worsens it.
Yes, for about a week now, whenever I stand up quickly or bend forward, the vision in both of my eyes goes completely black for two or three seconds before clearing up.
My peripheral vision feels slightly blurred, and I have had occasional double vision side-by-side when looking far to the left or right, but no eye redness or pain with eye movement.
Yes, I hear a rhythmic whooshing or beating sound in both ears, like rushing water that pulses in time with my heartbeat, especially at night.
I occasionally feel queasy and nauseous when the headache is at its worst, but I have not vomited.
Bright lights can bother my eyes when the headache is severe, but normal sounds do not trouble me.
No, I have not had any eye tearing, eye redness, nasal congestion, runny nose, or drooping of my eyelids.
No, I have not had any fever, chills, night sweats, or skin rashes.
No, my neck moves freely and does not feel stiff or painful at all.
No, I have not had any weakness or numbness in my arms or legs, speech problems, dizziness, or seizures.
No, I have not bumped my head, fallen, or had any recent trauma.
I tried taking acetaminophen and ibuprofen three to four times a week, but they barely made a dent in the pressure.
I have not noticed triggers like certain foods, wine, or missed meals; straining and lying flat seem to be the only things that clearly worsen it.
I have gained about ten kilograms over the past nine months because my work schedule changed and I became much less physically active.
No one else at home has headaches, and we do not use any gas heaters, coal stoves, or unventilated heating appliances.
No, I have never been diagnosed with cancer, HIV, or any autoimmune disease, and I do not take immunosuppressive drugs.
I keep worrying that I have a brain tumor or some dangerous eye condition that's causing these blackouts.
I'm terrified that these vision blackouts are going to become permanent and leave me completely blind.
I hope you can send me for a brain scan right away and connect me with an eye specialist today.
I do not have high blood pressure, diabetes, thyroid disease, or any other chronic medical conditions.
I have never had any surgeries and I have never been hospitalized.
I do not take any prescription medications, birth control pills, acne medicines like isotretinoin, tetracycline antibiotics, or vitamin A supplements.
I have no known allergies to any medications, foods, or materials.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used any tobacco or vaping products.
I only drink a glass of wine socially once or twice a month, and I do not drink heavily.
I work as an accountant at an office, sitting at a desk most of the day, and I live with my husband in an apartment.
My periods are regular every twenty-eight days, my last menstrual period was two weeks ago, we use barrier contraception, and there is no possibility I am pregnant.
There is no family history of brain tumors, aneurysms, blood clots, or chronic neurological disorders.

exam.finding: Blood pressure is 124/78 mmHg, heart rate is 74 beats per minute, respiratory rate is 14 breaths per minute, body temperature is 36.6°C, and oxygen saturation is 99% on ambient air.
Alert, moderately overweight female who appears mildly uncomfortable from head pain but in no acute distress.

Funduscopy demonstrates bilateral papilledema with blurred optic disc margins and optic disc swelling; pupils are equal, round, and briskly reactive to light, with enlarged blind spots on visual field confrontation.
Mild bilateral abducens nerve (CN VI) paresis with slight limitation on lateral gaze; other cranial nerves II through XII are completely intact.
Supple neck with full passive and active range of motion; Kernig and Brudzinski signs are negative.
Normal muscle bulk and tone with 5/5 motor strength in all muscle groups across bilateral upper and lower extremities.
Intact light touch, pinprick, vibration, and position sense symmetrically across all extremities.
Bilateral biceps, triceps, patellar, and Achilles reflexes are 2+ and symmetric; plantar responses are flexor bilaterally.
Intact finger-to-nose and rapid alternating movements bilaterally; gait is steady and narrow-based with a negative Romberg test.
No tenderness on palpation over the frontal or maxillary sinuses, and temporal arteries are non-tender and pulsatile without nodularity.
